summary: At the pool of Bethesda, Jesus heals a man ill for thirty-eight years on the Sabbath, then answers His accusers by claiming to work as His Father works.
key_insight: Jesus did not defend the healing by arguing that it was allowed. He said, “My Father has been working until now, and I have been working.” His opponents understood Him exactly: He was claiming God’s own right to work on the Sabbath.
story: Some time later there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. Near the Sheep Gate was a pool called in Hebrew Bethesda, with five porches. Under them lay a great multitude of sick people, blind, lame and paralyzed, “waiting for the moving of the water.”

One man there had been ill for thirty-eight years. When Jesus saw him lying there and knew he had been that way a long time, He asked him, “Do you want to be made well?” The man answered, “Sir, I have no man to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up; but while I am coming, another steps down before me.”
Jesus said to him, “Rise, take up your bed and walk.” Immediately the man was made well, picked up his mat and walked. And that day was the Sabbath.

The Jewish leaders stopped him: “It is the Sabbath; it is not lawful for you to carry your bed.” He told them that the man who healed him had told him to carry it, but he could not say who it was, because Jesus had slipped away into the crowd. Later Jesus found him in the temple and said, “See, you have been made well. Sin no more, lest a worse thing come upon you.” The man went and told the leaders that it was Jesus.

From then on the leaders persecuted Jesus because He did these things on the Sabbath. Jesus answered them, “My Father has been working until now, and I have been working.” Now they wanted to kill Him all the more. In their eyes He broke the Sabbath and also called God His own Father, “making Himself equal with God.”

Jesus did not take back a word. “Most assuredly, I say to you, the Son can do nothing of Himself, but what He sees the Father do.” The Father loves the Son and shows Him all He does. As the Father raises the dead, so the Son gives life to whom He will. The Father has committed all judgment to the Son, “that all should honor the Son just as they honor the Father.” Whoever hears His word and believes the One who sent Him “has everlasting life, and shall not come into judgment, but has passed from death into life.” The hour was coming when all in the graves would hear His voice and come out.

Then Jesus called His witnesses. John the Baptist had borne witness to the truth, “the burning and shining lamp.” The works the Father gave Him to do testified that the Father had sent Him. The Father Himself had testified. And the Scriptures they searched so carefully were the very ones “which testify of Me.” “But you are not willing to come to Me that you may have life.”
He ended with a warning. He would not need to accuse them before the Father; Moses, the one they trusted, would do that. “For if you believed Moses, you would believe Me; for he wrote about Me.”

scene.label: The pool
scene.text: Excavations north of the temple area, near the Church of St. Anne, uncovered two large pools divided by a wide rock wall. Covered walkways on the four sides and one across the middle would explain John’s “five porches.” The Sheep Gate stood nearby (Nehemiah 3:1), probably where sheep for the temple were brought in.

scene.label: Verse 4
scene.text: The NKJV includes the end of verse 3 and all of verse 4, about an angel stirring the water, and notes that some of the oldest manuscripts do not have them. Verse 7, which all manuscripts have, shows what the sick believed: the first one into the stirred water would be healed.

scene.label: Carrying on the Sabbath
scene.text: Through Jeremiah, God had forbidden carrying burdens out of houses or through Jerusalem’s gates on the Sabbath (Jeremiah 17:21–22). Jewish tradition, later written down in the Mishnah, went further and counted carrying any object from a house into the street, or from one such area to another, as forbidden work. A sleeping mat carried through the city broke their rule.

scene.label: God never stops working
scene.text: Jewish teachers of the period, and later rabbis, held that God Himself does not stop working on the Sabbath: He keeps the world going, giving life and judging. Jesus claimed that same freedom, and in the discourse He names those two works, giving life and judging, as His own (5:21–22).

scene.label: Two or three witnesses
scene.text: The Law required two or three witnesses to establish a matter (Deuteronomy 19:15), so one man’s word about himself settled nothing. That is why Jesus says His own witness alone would not stand, and then calls four: John, His works, the Father and the Scriptures.

witnesses.john: John alone tells this sign, as he alone records most of Jesus’ visits to Jerusalem, and he does not name the feast. He uses the healing to open the first long dispute in Jerusalem, where Jesus claims equality with the Father and calls His witnesses. From here John shows the plot to kill Jesus hardening (5:18; 7:1).

seeing.reveals: Jesus works as His Father works. He gives life by His word, holds the judgment of all people, and asks for the same honor that is given to the Father.
seeing.living: The leaders searched the Scriptures and still would not come to Jesus for life (5:39–40). Read the Bible to meet Him, not only to know about Him, and honor the Son as you honor the Father.
seeing.ponder: When you open the Scriptures, do you come to Jesus Himself, or only to the pages that tell about Him?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus works as the Father works: He gives life by His word.
outline: A question for a man who had waited (1–7)
A word that did what the water could not (8–9)
A Sabbath work only God can claim (10–18)
Life and judgment in the Son’s hands (19–24)
preaching.watch_for: The word “work” ties the chapter together. The healed man may not carry his bed, yet the Father works and the Son works (5:17), and the Father will show the Son “greater works than these” (5:20; see 5:36).
